newsitem.title: LIBERIA: Reprieve for relief aid in south west Liberia.
newsitem.headline: Reprieve for relief aid in south west Liberia.

text.p: International relief groups in Liberia agreed on Monday to resume humanitarian aid missions halted by faction violence in south west Cape Mount region but said they would monitor security there on a daily basis.

U.N. spokesman Kent Page said aid groups had agreed to resume convoys to civilians in the region after an assessment team visited the town of Sinje and received no form of harassment. He gave no time frame for the resumption.

"We all got together for a very intense meeting with all the representatives of the humanitarian community and it was decided that humanitarian relief operations will continue in the area," he told British Broadcasting Corporation radio.
"We are going to closely monitor the security situation on the ground on a daily basis. There remain many malnourished children and medically ill people who need the assistance that we can provide."
Aid groups called a halt to convoys on Sunday, pending the result of Monday's assessment mission.
A relief team that visited Sinje, 100 km (60 miles) west of the capital Monrovia, at the weekend after an attack by one of two rival factions reported scenes of death and looting.
"We were shown a pile of dead bodies of civilians," Martha Carey, country director of Medecins Sans Frontieres, said, describing them as women and children aged 10 to 15.
"Civilians we found on the road just outside town said their wives and children with their food rations had been taken away by the fighters."
Page reported seeing civilians fleeing, some wounded, fresh graves and a girl of eight months whose foot had been hacked off.
Fighters from the initially allied but now rival ethnic Krahn and Mandingo factions of the ULIMO group have been vying for control of the area for months.
The two groups fought on opposite sides during a flare-up in the civil war in Monrovia in April and May.
Relief groups, who found hundreds of starving children in the western town of Tubmanburg in early September, supplied Cape Mount for the first time in months last week.

In Monrovia, the interim ruling Council of State and the West African peacekeeping force ECOMOG held separate meetings to decide what to do about the fighting. The two rival factions had earlier pledged safe passage for relief convoys.

Over the weekend, faction leader Charles Taylor, who launched the war in 1989 and whose supporters fought alongside the Mandingo wing of ULIMO in April and May, showed U.N. special envoy Anthony Nyakyi an assembly point for 550 fighters near his Gbarnga stronghold.

Taylor commanders said the fighters' weapons had been taken away and would be handed over to the peacekeepers. Taylor himself called for a proper programme for demobilised fighters, many of them little more than children.
Freed American slaves set up Liberia in 1847. The war has killed well over 150,000 people, many of them civilians.

West African leaders, frustrated by a dozen collapsed peace deals, brokered a new agreement in August backed by the threat of individual sanctions against any faction leader derailing it. It envisages disarmament by January and elections by May.
